correctness.rationale: For each vertex, the maximum degree in its closed neighborhood is its component order minus one, since every connected trivially perfect component has a universal vertex. Two refinement rounds therefore separate component orders. Induct on maximum component order, restricting the stable equitable partition first to the smaller components, and then to the nonuniversal parts R of the largest components. Both restrictions are to unions of cells. On R the restricted partition refines the stable partition of R, so equal colours imply an orbit of Aut(R), not necessarily equality of these partitions. For two universal classes of equal colour, neighbor counts in the global universal union recover equal numbers of universals, and counts in the Aut(R)-orbits recover multiplicities of each nonuniversal component type. Thus their full parent components are isomorphic. Equal colours of two nonuniversal vertices give equal parent universal colours by equitability and the same pointed component type in R by induction. An isomorphism between their nonuniversal parts can send the chosen point to the chosen point by matching the remaining component types; inside one parent it is a component permutation with suitable internal isomorphisms. This yields a full-graph automorphism. Automorphism invariance gives the converse, with the empty graph vacuous. The 2K3 versus C6 comparison correctly concerns amenability, not internal orbits. The frozen atlas/forest/nonamenable programs and outputs were inspected, not executed; the universal result is established by the induction.

value.rationale: This gives exact automorphism information from an elementary uniform refinement procedure throughout a natural hereditary graph class, including repeated connected components without individualization. It identifies the signal that carries component and pointed-type information and sharply distinguishes internal orbit recovery from unrestricted identification. This is a structural all-order theorem, not a finite success report or an application of the known hierarchy alone.
